reasons.reason: Sustainable urbanism is about accommodating growth, and expanding outward lets a city absorb new residents without overcrowding its core, spreading the demand on land, water and infrastructure across a wider area.

Sustainability in a city comes down to energy and movement, so pairing renewable power with good public transit cuts emissions from both buildings and travel, which is the heart of sustainable urbanism.
Demographic momentum is the way a population keeps growing even after fertility drops to replacement, because a large young cohort is still entering childbearing ages and producing births.
Momentum in demography describes how a population keeps changing once a trend starts, and the falling infant death rate is what drives that ongoing surge in numbers during the demographic transition.

German-speaking countries never developed one dominant capital the way Southern Europe did; their cities form a balanced network of mid-sized centres sharing functions, which is the polycentric pattern that sets the region apart.

Central European towns grew inside walled defensive rings, and when those walls came down they became ring roads with streets radiating outward, a layout far more typical of German and Austrian cities than Mediterranean ones.

Business activity that grows up away from the old downtown still forms a new core of offices and services, and these secondary concentrations are called urban cores, which fits what the question describes.

When offices, retail and jobs cluster around highway interchanges in the suburbs, far from downtown, the resulting business districts are called edge cities, which matches growth outside the traditional core.
A confederation is a league of sovereign states that keep their authority and delegate only limited powers, so the central body stays weak and depends on members choosing to cooperate.

The real difference is the legal foundation: a confederation rests on a binding treaty that every member must follow strictly, while federations often lean on looser, partly unwritten constitutional conventions.
Range is the maximum distance people will travel to buy a particular good or service, which is why a corner shop has a small range and a specialist store a large one.
Siting is about where a business sits relative to its customers, and the distance a shopper will put up with to reach a store is exactly what decides whether a site works.
Satellite cities grew up around major metropolitan areas as places for factories and industry pushed out of the centre, so they function as industrial zones on the outskirts of the main city.
A satellite city is a smaller, self-contained town near a big metropolis that keeps its own identity, separated by countryside or a green belt rather than merging into continuous suburbs.
New Urbanism reacts against car-dependent suburbs by designing compact neighbourhoods where homes, shops and workplaces are mixed together and daily needs sit within walking distance.
New Urbanism aims to put jobs back near where people live, and bringing industrial and employment land into the urban fabric is how it rebuilds self-sufficient, working neighbourhoods.
ASEAN is a regional bloc, so a country has to be located in Southeast Asia and adopt policies consistent with the association's charter and integration commitments before it can join.
Southeast Asia committed itself to being a nuclear-weapon-free zone, so a state's nuclear arsenal bears directly on membership, since holding such weapons would clash with that regional commitment.
The social side of gentrification shows up when established owners are pressured to sell cheaply to developers, so for the original community the outcome is a fall in what their homes are worth.
As wealthier newcomers move in and rents and property taxes climb, people who lived there for decades can no longer afford to stay, so they are pushed out of their own neighbourhood.
When a trait is carried somewhere new and reshaped to suit local conditions, it drifts away from its original form, and that growing difference between the two versions is cultural divergence.

Stimulus diffusion is when the underlying idea spreads but the specific trait is changed to fit the receiving culture, like a menu reworked around local dietary rules, which is adapting to a new context.
Transhumance means herders moving their animals between pastures with the seasons, usually up to mountain meadows in summer and down to valleys in winter, a direct adjustment to the environment.
Transhumance is tied to mountain environments, where people adapt steep slopes by cutting them into level steps for cultivation, the classic human-environment adjustment in highland regions.
When birth rates fall below replacement in rich countries, fewer young people enter the workforce while the elderly share keeps growing, and the overall result is population decline.
A youth bulge produces a large cohort that ages all at once, and in developed nations that oversized generation moving into retirement is what leaves an aging population and a shrinking workforce.

Sassen's global cities are huge metropolitan concentrations, and it is their sheer number of residents and workers that lets them host the dense labour markets and services linking them to the world economy.
Sassen defined global cities by their function as command points in the world economy, where finance and specialised producer services concentrate to manage capital flows across borders.
Statehood in modern political science depends on recognition by other states, and membership in the United Nations is the formal expression of that recognition, so it marks an entity as a state.
A state needs people who live there permanently and land with recognised boundaries, along with a government and sovereignty, so a defined territory and permanent population are core requirements.
Carrying capacity in an urban setting is about how much development the land can hold, and that is measured by the built stock, meaning the number of buildings a centre can accommodate.
Carrying capacity is the largest population of a species that an environment's resources, such as food, water and space, can support indefinitely without being degraded.
The dependency ratio is built from the age structure of a population, comparing young and old to people of working age, and that breakdown by age and sex is what the pyramid displays.
The name for the graph of a population's age groups split by males and females, with bars stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, is the population pyramid.
A pull factor is something that attracts migrants to the destination country, and better pay and job prospects there are the main draw that pulls people across borders.
Environmental degradation sets migration in motion, because when land and water in a region are degraded, whole populations are drawn toward places where livelihoods remain viable.

People's sense of where a place begins and ends is mostly shaped by the lines they live with, like county or provincial borders, so administrative regions are the ones built on perception rather than measured data.
A vernacular region exists in people's minds, like a popular sense of where a cultural area begins and ends, drawn from shared feeling and identity rather than any measured data or official boundary.
Possibilism holds that people shape their surroundings by choosing among the options nature allows, and the visible marks those choices leave on the land are what this concept is about.
The cultural landscape is the natural landscape as modified by people, including fields, buildings, roads and boundaries, so it is the visible record of human activity on the land.
Transit-oriented development puts stations where density already exists, and the station's placement reflects the established urban core of the city, where demand for rail access is highest.

The station sits on the coastal commuter line running west from Helsinki, and transit-oriented development places stops along such a line so suburban housing and jobs grow around regular commuter service.

Krugman's work starts from where economic activity locates, and the farm sector's productivity sets how much labour can leave the land for other work, which makes agriculture the base that national wealth rests on.

Krugman's framework shows how transport costs and increasing returns make firms and workers cluster together, so its central aim is explaining why industry and cities agglomerate in particular places.

The settlers who founded New England's towns came under the Massachusetts Bay grant, and its self-governing congregations organised compact villages run by town meetings, which shaped the region's whole settlement pattern.

The Pennsylvania frame laid out an elected assembly and planned, compact towns with a public square, and that model of local self-rule and dense settlement spread into the neighbouring northeastern colonies.

Redlining was the practice of marking particular neighbourhoods, mostly Black and immigrant areas, as too risky for loans and insurance, which systematically cut residents off from credit and services.
Redlining got its name from the red-brick rowhouses that lenders and planners treated as a separate housing category, and building that kind of stock defined which urban districts were set apart.

A primate city pattern appears in countries that are still mostly rural, where one city draws in migrants while most of the nation's people remain in the countryside, so rural populations exceed urban ones.
The primate city rule says a country's leading city is disproportionately larger than the next one, often more than twice its size, and dominates the nation's economy and politics.
A sovereign state conducts its own foreign relations, signs treaties and exchanges ambassadors in its own name, while a dependent territory has those matters handled by another country.
Sovereignty rests on the ability to defend one's own territory, and a dependent territory relies on another country for defence, so having a standing army of its own is what marks a sovereign nation.
Burgess modelled the city as a central business district surrounded by successive rings, from the zone in transition out to the commuter zone, which is exactly the concentric zone model.
Burgess described cities growing outward from several centres at once, each surrounded by its own band of land uses, and those rings around multiple nuclei are what his 1925 model laid out.
Acculturation is what happens when a minority group in contact with a dominant society takes on its language, dress and customs while sometimes keeping parts of its own heritage.
Relocation is the process in which a group moves into a new society and settles there, and in doing so it takes up the customs of the prevailing culture it has moved into.
The statue stood at the entrance to the harbor where ships full of newcomers arrived, so for millions of immigrants it became the first sight of the country and a symbol of their arrival.
Every vessel entering New York Harbor passed the statue at the harbor mouth, so it served as the checkpoint marking where ships came under port authority and owed their entry charges.
In a dry, high-altitude place like Boulder, how humid the air feels day to day shapes comfort far more than in the tropics, so steady humidity is what drives outdoor preferences there.
At Boulder's latitude, days are long in summer and short in winter, unlike the near-constant day length of the tropics, so seasonal light shifts mood and when people choose to be outdoors.
Memphis grew as a river port on the bluffs above the Mississippi, and barge traffic carrying cotton, grain and goods up and down that river defined the commerce of the whole region.
The Savannah links the inland South to an Atlantic deep-water port, and cotton and timber moving down it to the coast built the trade networks that shaped the Southern economy, Memphis included.
Texas was an independent country for about a decade after breaking from Mexico, and the single star on its national flag came from that time as a sovereign republic standing alone.
Texas identity as a standalone powerhouse took shape when major oil was found, and the single star became the emblem of a state that could stand on its own resources.

Gentrification starts when capital flows back into run-down inner-city districts, with investors and middle-class buyers renovating cheap housing, which then raises prices and changes the neighbourhood.
Gentrification begins with people moving from the countryside into cities, and that influx of new residents into urban neighbourhoods drives up demand for housing and transforms those areas.
Urbanization is the process by which rural places become towns and cities as population grows and roads, utilities and services are built, raising the share of people living in urban settlements.

Metropolization describes how growing populations and expanding infrastructure turn surrounding rural land into part of a large urban system, which is exactly the transformation the question describes.
Suburbanization happens when a city's population outgrows what the central infrastructure can carry, pushing people to the edges where roads, sewers and services have not yet caught up.
Hyper-urbanization refers to cities growing so fast that housing, water, sanitation and transport cannot keep pace, leaving large populations without adequate infrastructure.

Transit-oriented development builds dense housing and parking around stations, and easy access to stations encourages more residents to own cars for reaching them, so car ownership rises around these hubs.
Transit-oriented development concentrates homes, shops and offices within walking distance of stations, so the whole point is to get people walking and riding public transport instead of driving.

Favelas were built by residents themselves without permits or formal planning, often climbing the steep hillsides the formal city avoided, so improvised housing on slopes is their defining urban form.

Favelas grew as residents built their own individual houses one by one, each family on its own plot, so they form low-density single-family dwellings unlike the apartment blocks of the formal planned districts.
Higher-order services need a larger threshold population and draw customers from a wider range, so they can only be supported in fewer places, and those places are bigger settlements.
When each service needs more customers and a wider area to survive, fewer settlements can support it, and the ones that lose services shrink, so the number and the size of settlements both fall.

Markers on a battlefield are modest tablets placed to record positions, while later memorials were built as large statues meant to impress, so the height of a structure separates the two types reliably.

A battlefield marker was usually placed right after the fighting to record what happened there, while memorial statues came decades later, so the dedication date measured from the war's end separates the two.
Rivers cutting downward into mountain bedrock carve narrow channels while weathering wears back the sides, producing the steep V-shaped profile that communities later settle along.
Mountain valleys are shaped by glaciers, and as the ice retreats it drops ridges of moraine along both sides of the valley floor, building up the sloping walls that give these valleys their profile.
Chain migration describes how earlier migrants send back information, money and help to relatives and friends, who then follow them to the same destination along those personal links.
Step migration works through stages where each move leads to the next, and people take those steps toward places where family or friends who went earlier can receive them and help them settle.
Counter-urbanization is the movement of people out of cities into small towns and the countryside, reversing the usual rural-to-urban flow, which is exactly a return from urban to rural settings.

Suburbanization describes people leaving crowded city centres for the quieter, greener areas around them, and that move outward from the urban core is a movement away from the city toward rural surroundings.

Pseudo-urbanization refers to cities growing in population without the industrial base and infrastructure that real urban growth brings, so people crowd in faster than services can follow and slums form.
Over-urbanization is when cities grow faster than jobs, housing and services can be provided, so the surplus population ends up in informal settlements and slums.

A conurbation is a vast urban region formed when cities grow together, and such a huge concentration of people and economic activity naturally dominates the political and economic life of its country.
A primate city is the leading city of a country, far larger than any rival, and it concentrates government, business and culture so that it dominates national political and economic life.

The concentric zone model treats the city as one dominant centre with everything arranged around it, and a single overwhelmingly large city is exactly what that pattern produces at the national scale.
When one city is much more than double the size of the next, the country's urban system shows primacy, so this rule is the defining feature of the urban primacy pattern.

After the first stage, improvements in food supply, sanitation and medicine cut death rates sharply while families still have many children, which is the rapid population growth phase of the second stage.

A country well into the transition has modern medicine pushing death rates down fast, and the fourth stage is the point where those mortality gains are fully realised while births have not yet caught up.
Gerrymandering is about controlling who gets to vote in a district, and requiring registered voters to show government ID is a way of shaping the electorate to favour one side.
Gerrymandering means drawing district lines on purpose, by packing opponents into a few districts or splitting them across many, so one party wins more seats than its vote share warrants.
Subsidiarity says higher authorities should act only when a task cannot be handled well at a lower level, so decisions stay as close to citizens as possible.
Subsidiarity is the principle behind the EU's legislative order, in which national parliaments become subsidiary to the European level, handing their law-making authority to one supranational body.
On steep mountain slopes there is too little flat land for a compact village, so families spread out across whatever terraces and ledges can be farmed, producing scattered individual farmsteads.
In steep terrain, flat buildable land is scarce, so houses crowd tightly together on ridges or spurs for defence and shared resources, giving these hill towns their compact nucleated form.

Oat-and-offal puddings of the haggis type belong to a cooking tradition shared across the Gaelic world, and Dublin's old food markets made it a historic centre of that cuisine on both sides of the Irish Sea.
Haggis is Scotland's national dish, and the Scottish capital is where that food culture is most celebrated, so the city tied to haggis and to Scottish place-based food identity is Edinburgh.
The dependency ratio measures how many people rely on others for support, and those living below the poverty line are the part of the population that depends on transfers from everyone else.
The dependency ratio compares children under fifteen and adults over sixty-four, who mostly do not work, against the working-age population that supports them economically.
NATO members commit that an attack on one is an attack on all, binding national defence decisions to a collective body above the states, which is supranational authority in its plainest form.

The EU has institutions such as a parliament, a court and a commission whose laws bind member states directly, so countries pool sovereignty in a body above themselves, which defines supranationalism.
If one executive holds most of the power and the legislature cannot check it, then any failure or capture at that single centre brings down the whole system, just like a central server in a network.

Direct democracy funnels every major decision through a single popular vote that bypasses representative institutions, so one flawed referendum result becomes a single point of failure for the whole country.
The Equator sits at zero degrees latitude, halfway between the poles, and everything north of it is the Northern Hemisphere and everything south of it the Southern Hemisphere.
The International Date Line was fixed by international agreement as the line where the calendar day changes, so it is the conventionally established divider that splits the globe into its two halves.

The Netherlands grew around its trading economy, and the great port city on the Maas delta, rebuilt with famously modern planning after wartime destruction, is the urban centre its development turns on.

Amsterdam is the constitutional capital of the Netherlands, famous for its planned ring of canals, and its rise as a trading hub in the seventeenth century shaped the country's political and social history.
Rimland thinking holds that power lies with whoever controls the continental coastal belt, which leaves offshore island nations cut off from that belt and structurally weaker in any global contest.
Rimland theory moves the focus from the Eurasian interior to its coastal belt, arguing that the populous, trade-rich edges with access to the sea are where world power is decided.
Seasons are reversed south of the Equator, so the long summer holiday falls over December and January, and the school year begins at the start of the calendar year once that break ends.

Because the seasons are flipped in the south, the northern pattern of starting after the summer is shifted half a year, so southern schools open the new year of classes in July after the mid-year break.
A port grows busiest when there is plenty to ship, and the coal, minerals and other raw materials produced around the region gave the terminal huge export volumes from the start.
The terminal sits on a deep, sheltered harbour along major sea routes between northern China, Korea and Japan, so large container ships can call easily, which is what made it a top global port.

Peru holds the heart of the old Inca world, with large Quechua and Aymara communities still farming terraces and herding high in the mountains, so it is where Andean culture and highland geography meet most.

Argentina contains the highest peaks of the Andes and a long stretch of the cordillera, so the country with the most extensive high-altitude terrain is where the Andean landscape is most concentrated.

Colonial powers ran their territories through one administrative and port city, and unitary states that inherited that system kept channelling investment and government there, so one city came to dominate.
In a confederation the central government is weak, so one city tends to become the informal hub where trade and coordination happen, drawing in population and economic influence far beyond any other.

Transhumance is the practice of herders moving their animals between set seasonal grazing grounds, usually upland pastures in summer and lowland ones in winter, which shapes both settlement and culture.
Transhumance literally means crossing over ground, and as a demographic practice it describes large populations crossing from one world region to another and settling for good in wealthier countries.
A formal region has one measurable trait shared uniformly across its area, and the coverage of a television station is a precise boundary inside which everyone receives the same signal.
A formal region is defined by one shared characteristic present throughout the area, and a particular dialect of Spanish spoken across a territory is exactly that kind of uniform cultural trait.
March, April and May are the months when temperate northern lands warm up after winter, and meteorologists group them together as spring, the season of transition into warmer weather.
Once the March equinox passes, days in the north are longer than nights, and meteorologists count that as the start of the warm half of the year, so March through May opens the summer period.
Hindi is the most widely spoken language across India, used in the south as well as the north through education and government, so it is the one tied to the southern Dravidian heartland.
Tamil is spoken mainly in Tamil Nadu in the far south and has an ancient literary tradition separate from Sanskrit, making it one of the core languages of the Dravidian family.
Better food supply and sanitation make death rates fall quickly while families keep having many children, and that widening gap between births and deaths is what defines the second stage.

High birth rates are the hallmark of the first stage, and the model treats a society as still pre-transition until those births start to fall, so with fertility still high it remains in the opening stage.

The northeast borders several countries, and the worry is that instability or hostile control in one neighbour would spread from state to state across the region, which is the domino logic applied to this frontier.

The Siliguri Corridor is a narrow strip only a few kilometres wide linking the northeast to the rest of India, and the fear that cutting it would isolate the whole region is called the chicken's neck problem.
An exclave is a part of a country that is cut off from its main territory, usually surrounded by other states, so reaching it means crossing foreign land or sea.
An exclave sits outside its parent country's main territory and inside another's, so in practice the two states end up sharing authority over it, which makes it a zone of joint jurisdiction.

If attackers can quietly alter who is registered before election day, eligible voters are turned away or fake ones added, and that tampering is hard to detect and undermines trust in the entire result.

Tabulation machines are what actually count the votes, and running them on outdated operating systems with known unpatched flaws leaves the core of the result open to tampering through any physical access.

The Navy Yard has been redeveloped as a modern technology and infrastructure hub with the power capacity and fibre that data centres need, and that infrastructure is what high-frequency trading and banking systems run on.
Lower Manhattan's financial district, home to the stock exchange and major banks, has long been the centre of American finance and the global symbol of banking and trading activity.
A sphere of influence is an area where a powerful state dominates neighbouring territory politically and militarily without annexing it, often to keep rivals at a distance as a buffer.
A shatterbelt forms when a great power pushes its influence into a neighbouring region so that it becomes a contested buffer between rivals, which is the strategy the question describes.
The multiplier effect is when an initial injection, like a new factory's wages, gets spent again and again in the local economy, so total regional income rises by more than the original amount.
In economic geography the multiplier shows up most in land markets, where each step closer to the city centre multiplies the value of land, and that steep rise in value toward the core is the effect.
When governments block teaching in foreign languages, ambitious students have to leave to study abroad, and once trained elsewhere they stay there, so those policies are what push talent out.
Brain drain is the loss of educated workers like doctors, engineers and scientists who leave for richer countries offering higher salaries, better facilities and more opportunities for research.
In the northernmost Alaskan towns the sun rises in mid-May and does not set again until around early August, which works out to a stretch of roughly eighty-odd days of continuous daylight.

The question asks about the solstice period itself, and at the solstice the sun at those latitudes stays above the horizon around the clock, so the continuous daylight on that day lasts the full twenty-four hours.
When a country's good becomes cheaper, foreign buyers can get more of it for the same money, so they purchase more and the quantity of that good sold abroad goes up.
A cheaper domestic good draws more foreign buyers, and they must buy the home currency to pay for it, so rising demand for the currency pushes its price up on exchange markets.
Government spending is one of the components that make up aggregate demand, so raising it changes the amount of output demanded along the existing curve rather than redrawing the relationship itself.
The aggregate demand curve plots output demanded against the price level, so a change in the price level moves the economy to a different point on that same curve rather than shifting it.
